title: Financial Policy Committee Record – April 2026
summary: The FPC met on 27 March 2026 and judged that the Middle East conflict has resulted in a substantial negative supply shock, triggering large and volatile moves in global energy prices and government bond yields. The Committee identified multiple interconnected vulnerabilities across sovereign debt markets, private credit, and AI-related systemic risks that could crystallise simultaneously and amplify financial stability concerns. The FPC maintained the UK CCyB rate at 2%,judging the banking system remains appropriately capitalised and capable of supporting households and businesses even under substantially worse conditions.
key_points: The Middle East conflict has created a negative supply shock increasing risks to financial stability through higher energy prices, inflation, and tighter financial conditions.

Sovereign debt markets face historically high issuance with higher proportions at shorter maturities, compounded by concentrated leverage among hedge funds pursuing similar strategies across jurisdictions—increasing disorderly unwind risk.
Repo markets have functioned to absorb volatility so far, providing a market structure buffer, though fragility remains.
Private credit markets show liquidity concerns with elevated redemption requests in retail funds and valuation uncertainty, particularly for software and services exposed companies.
The FPC reiterated support for the Private Markets System-wide Exploratory Scenario (PM SWES) to assess bank and NBFI dynamics in private markets under stress.
The CCyB rate was maintained at 2%; no evidence of banks restricting lending to protect capital positions despite increased macro risks.
Financial system participants have not yet adopted advanced AI (generative or agentic) in a systemic risk manner, but risks are likely to increase as adoption expands.
why_it_matters: The FPC record provides an official financial stability risk assessment identifying specific structural vulnerabilities and amplification pathways. Market participants should incorporate stress scenarios involving sudden price adjustments given the materially more unpredictable global environment. The document signals active monitoring of hedge fund leverage in sovereign markets, private credit liquidity mismatches, and AI-related systemic risks—all relevant to trading, risk management, and regulatory compliance decisions.
macro_context: The supply shock from the Middle East conflict is expected to weigh on global growth while increasing inflation—creating a stagflationary dynamic that tightens financial conditions. Sovereign debt outlook has worsened through potential growth headwinds, higher rates, and increased government spending pressures. Private credit faces dual pressure from higher rates increasing debt-servicing costs and lower growth reducing asset quality.
market_structure_context: Repo markets have functioned to absorb high volatility and volumes, providing market infrastructure resilience. However, concentrated hedge fund leverage in sovereign debt across jurisdictions creates disorderly unwind and illiquidity jump risk. Private credit funds show liquidity mismatch through elevated redemptions and some fund gating. These dynamics highlight NBFI (non-bank financial institution) risks as a market structure concern.
